title: Martha, Mary
html_source:
Mary and Martha are sisters portrayed in the Gospels of Luke and John. In one story, Martha is practical, preparing Jesus’s dinner, but Mary sits at Jesus' feet listening to him. When Martha complains that Mary should help with the work, Jesus tells her to stop worrying, that Mary has made the better choice. Luke 10. This scene is depicted in the picture Bloom remembers in the next paragraph.

He refers to the Martha in the painting as “the other one,” despite mentioning her first, and observes she “was getting the supper.” Whereas he fantasizes about the dark eyed Mary in the painting listening to him rapturously.

There is something to the comparison of the biblical characters of Martha and Mary, and the Martha and Molly (Marion, a variation on Mary) in Bloom’s life.

Is it that Molly is languorous and Martha industrious? (“I do wish I could do something for you.”)

Is it irony that he has neither a Mary nor a Martha? That Bloom feels Molly is not enthralled by him, and that the grammatically challenged Martha could not be the typist he has advertised for?
